items.title: Peculiar family of recurrence formula where for $n>1$ if you take the $n$-th prime factor of each term, you get an eventually periodic sequence
items.body:
The particular family I'm describing is:

$$A_k = A_{k-1}B_{k-2}+A_{k-2}B_{k-1}$$ $$B_k = A_{k-1}B_{k-2}-A_{k-2}B_{k-1}$$ $$A_0 = B_0 = B_1 = 1$$ $$A_1 = N$$

We consider this family of sequence for integer $N>1$. Also, we would focus on $A$-sequence and we'll ignore the $B$-sequence for now.

I am experimenting by taking the $n$-th prime factor of each term. I notice something remarkable. For any of the $n$ and $N$ I choose, the sequence generated by this process seems to be an eventually periodic sequence.

Here's the cycle for some values of $n$ and $N$:

$n = 2, N = 2: (3, 5, 7)$ $n = 2, N = 3: (5, 3, 17)$ $n = 2, N = 4: (3, 7, 43)$ $n = 2, N = 5: (3, 7, 5)$ $n = 2, N = 6: (3, 5, 13)$ $n = 3, N = 2: (11, 19, 13)$ $n = 3, N = 3: (7, 19, 11)$ $n = 3, N = 4: (5, 11, 59)$ $n = 3, N = 5: (11, 23, 17)$ $n = 3, N = 6: (7, 23, 19)$

Interesting hmm... I couldn't think of anyway of proving that this periodicity holds for all values of $n$ and $N$. I am ignorant of higher-level mathematics, well, I'm only 16 years old who just started to take 1st-2nd year undergrad course, self-studying. I am guessing this might be something trivial, where I can understand the proof if given to me, I think the question might be for MSE... But proving this, I just can't think of any ways.
